cards.title: Algorithmic threshold for random k-SAT
cards.formal: Does the randomized polynomial-time satisfying-assignment threshold for random \(k\)-SAT satisfy \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)}{2^{k}\ln(k)/k}=1?\] For each fixed \(k\), \(\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)\) is the supremum of constant clause densities at which some polynomial-time algorithm finds a satisfying assignment with probability tending to one as the number \(n\) of variables tends to infinity. The distribution and quantifiers are specified below.

source_formulation.text: Given the existence of satisfying assignments for \(\alpha  = Ok (2k ), a\) natural algorithmic question arises: can we find such an assignment efficiently?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 4

cards.why: Pinpoints a possible computational barrier inside a regime where satisfying assignments typically exist. A resolution would clarify whether the geometry of random constraint problems predicts the power of arbitrary efficient algorithms, beyond individual heuristics and restricted computational models.
cards.status_note: Read the conference source and full July 2025 version, the Fix publisher abstract and author introduction, and the full low-degree definitions and principal theorem statements. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution for arbitrary polynomial-time assignment finding. The supremum definition spells out the source’s asymptotic algorithmic-threshold question. The source’s damaged saved density and its separate incidental logarithm typo are not used as mathematical definitions.

importance.reason: A central statistical-versus-computational gap in random constraint satisfaction, with rigorous algorithms and restricted barriers but no general matching lower bound. Existing score retained.

sentences: The input is a random conjunction of fixed-width clauses, with all literal positions sampled independently.
The algorithm must find an assignment satisfying every clause with probability tending to one.
The conjectured leading threshold is two to the clause width times its natural logarithm, divided by the width.
Known algorithms reach this scale, while satisfying assignments exist at substantially higher densities.
Existing overlap-gap and low-degree barriers do not establish optimality against every polynomial-time algorithm.

cards.definitions:
Fix an integer \(k\geq3\) and a real constant density \(\alpha\geq0\). On Boolean variables \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\), generate \(m=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\) ordered clauses. Each clause has \(k\) literal positions, each independently uniform among \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\neg x_{1},\ldots,\neg x_{n}\). The formula is the AND of these OR clauses. Sampling is with replacement: repeated literals, tautological clauses and repeated clauses are allowed.

The algorithm receives the entire explicit formula, with variable indices in binary, together with \(n\). It must output one full assignment in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) satisfying every clause. It may report failure otherwise. The input is sampled without conditioning on satisfiability and without planting or revealing any assignment.

A density \(\alpha\) is algorithmically attainable at width \(k\) if there is a classical randomized algorithm \(A\), with no advice depending on \(n\), such that its running time is bounded by a polynomial in the explicit input length and \(n\) on every input and random tape, and
\[\Pr_{\Phi,A}[A(\Phi)\text{ outputs a satisfying assignment of }\Phi]\longrightarrow1
\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.\]
The probability includes both the random formula and the algorithm's internal randomness. One fixed algorithm must work for all \(n\) at the chosen \(k,\alpha\). Its code, polynomial degree and constants may depend on those fixed parameters. They are not allowed to depend separately on each input length.

Let \(\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)\) be the supremum of all such densities. Attainment at the supremum is not required. First take \(n\to\infty\) at fixed \(k,\alpha\); only then consider the asymptotic behavior as \(k\to\infty\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This is a leading-order asymptotic question, not a request for an exact critical density at a particular small \(k\).

The target ranges over all randomized polynomial-time assignment-finding algorithms. It imposes no locality, stability, low-degree representation or restriction to a named heuristic. Deciding satisfiability without producing an assignment, satisfying only most clauses, or proving a barrier for a restricted algorithm family is a different guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed asymptotic equality, or refute it. The known algorithm gives the lower bound \(1-o_{k}(1)\) on the ratio, so the missing positive direction is the matching upper bound for all polynomial-time algorithms. A refutation must change the limiting leading-order behavior along arbitrarily large widths; an improvement confined to one fixed small width or a lower-order term does not suffice.

context_blocks.title: Existence persists to substantially higher densities
context_blocks.text: For sufficiently large fixed \(k\), the satisfiability threshold is known and is asymptotic to \(2^{k}\ln 2\). This is about existence of an assignment; it does not provide an efficient way to find one throughout that range.

context_blocks.title: An algorithm reaches the conjectured scale from below
context_blocks.text: Coja-Oghlan’s Fix algorithm finds a satisfying assignment with high probability below \((1-\varepsilon_{k})2^{k}\ln(k)/k\), where \(\varepsilon_{k}\to0\). Thus the conjecture asks whether its leading asymptotic scale is optimal among all polynomial-time algorithms.

context_blocks.title: Restricted lower bounds are evidence, with additional qualifications
context_blocks.text: Bresler and Huang prove a low-degree obstruction above a constant multiple of this scale; their main stated constant is about \(4.911\), and their appendix discusses improvements. Theorem 2.6 concerns a specified normalized polynomial representation and requires a quantitatively small failure probability, stronger than an arbitrary \(o(1)\) failure rate. Their local-algorithm theorem rules out much smaller success probabilities within a narrower class. Neither theorem covers all polynomial-time algorithms.

context_blocks.title: An overlap-gap threshold is not the full algorithmic threshold
context_blocks.text: The 2025 source explicitly retains the algorithmic conjecture. Its sharp geometric results for random SAT use growing clause width in the relevant exact-solution regime. They do not establish the fixed-width, all-algorithm upper bound asked here.

cards.context:
For sufficiently large fixed \(k\), the satisfiability threshold is known and is asymptotic to \(2^{k}\ln 2\). This is about existence of an assignment; it does not provide an efficient way to find one throughout that range.

Coja-Oghlan’s Fix algorithm finds a satisfying assignment with high probability below \((1-\varepsilon_{k})2^{k}\ln(k)/k\), where \(\varepsilon_{k}\to0\). Thus the conjecture asks whether its leading asymptotic scale is optimal among all polynomial-time algorithms.

Bresler and Huang prove a low-degree obstruction above a constant multiple of this scale; their main stated constant is about \(4.911\), and their appendix discusses improvements. Theorem 2.6 concerns a specified normalized polynomial representation and requires a quantitatively small failure probability, stronger than an arbitrary \(o(1)\) failure rate. Their local-algorithm theorem rules out much smaller success probabilities within a narrower class. Neither theorem covers all polynomial-time algorithms.

The 2025 source explicitly retains the algorithmic conjecture. Its sharp geometric results for random SAT use growing clause width in the relevant exact-solution regime. They do not establish the fixed-width, all-algorithm upper bound asked here.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
